title: Geofence Warrants & the Fourth Amendment
hook: Police can ask a tech company which phones were near a crime scene at a given hour — sweeping up everyone's location, not just a suspect's. In 2026 the Court said that's a 'search.'
key_points: A geofence warrant asks a tech company for the location data of every device within a drawn area during a set time window.
That sweeps in innocent bystanders' data along with any suspect's — the reverse of a normal, name-first warrant.
The Fourth Amendment requires a warrant, based on probable cause, for government 'searches.'
In June 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that using a geofence warrant is itself a Fourth Amendment 'search', per SCOTUSblog.
The ruling extends the logic of Carpenter v. United States (2018), which protected cellphone location records generally.
content_html: Most warrants start with a suspect: police identify a person, then ask a court for permission to search their phone, home, or records. A "geofence warrant" runs the process backward — police draw a location and time window on a map and ask a tech company (often Google) to hand over data on every device that passed through it, then work backward to a suspect.
extra_html: That reversal is exactly what raised the constitutional question: the Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable government "searches" and generally requires a warrant grounded in probable cause aimed at a specific target, not a dragnet sweep of anyone who happened to be nearby. In June 2026, SCOTUSblog's Amy Howe reports, the Supreme Court ruled that law enforcement's use of a geofence warrant is itself a Fourth Amendment search — meaning the practice must meet the Amendment's warrant and probable-cause standards. The Conversation frames the decision as an extension of Carpenter v. United States (2018), where the Court first held that cellphone location records deserve Fourth Amendment protection because they can reveal a detailed record of someone's movements. Geofencing takes that concern further, since a single request sweeps up location data on everyone in an area — not just the eventual suspect — putting bystanders' movements in front of police by default. (This card describes U.S. constitutional law specifically.)

flashcards.prompt: How does a geofence warrant work, and why is that different from a typical warrant?
flashcards.back_html: Police draw a location and time window and ask a company for every device's data inside it, then work backward to a suspect — the reverse of starting with a named suspect.

flashcards.prompt: What did the Supreme Court rule about geofence warrants in June 2026?

choices.text: Using one is itself a Fourth Amendment 'search', so it must meet warrant and probable-cause standards
Geofence warrants are not searches and need no warrant at all
Only federal agencies may use geofence warrants

flashcards.explanation_html: The Court held the practice counts as a Fourth Amendment search, triggering the Amendment's usual protections.

flashcards.prompt: Which earlier case does this 2026 ruling extend the logic of?

choices.text: Carpenter v. United States (2018), on cellphone location records
Miranda v. Arizona, on the right to remain silent
Brown v. Board of Education, on school segregation

flashcards.explanation_html: Carpenter first held cellphone location data deserves Fourth Amendment protection; this ruling applies that logic to geofence warrants.
